Name: novelty_satiation_gating
Title: Bored of Its Own Ideas: A Novelty-Satiation Signal That Prematurely Collapses Exploration in Reasoning Models
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the curiosity/novelty-satiation phenomenon from human exploration science, we hypothesize that when a reasoning model generates candidate solution ideas within one chain of thought, an internal novelty signal decays as similar ideas accumulate, and once this signal drops below threshold the model stops proposing genuinely new approaches—committing early to a familiar strategy even on problems that require a different one. This premature exploration collapse is caused by a decodable, monotonically-satiating novelty representation whose early decay predicts failure; steering the novelty signal back up restores exploration and improves accuracy on problems the model otherwise abandons after one idea.
Related Work: Recent work shows LLMs explore poorly because they 'think too fast'—relying on early uncertainty-driven strategies and neglecting later empowerment signals, with SAE analysis showing uncertainty is represented in early layers (Large Language Models Think Too Fast To Explore Effectively, 2025); episode/anatomy analyses (ThinkARM, ReJump, Cognitive Foundations, 2025) show exploration is a critical branching point where correct solutions route into monitoring/re-analysis while incorrect ones continue execution or terminate; and The Illusion of Thinking (2025) documents effort collapse on hard problems. Curiosity work characterizes information-seeking and novelty-driven exploration in humans and RL (Computational mechanisms of curiosity, 2019; Curiosity-driven exploration, 2021) and even measures curiosity questionnaires in LLMs (Why Did Apple Fall, 2025). Crucially, NONE studies a within-trace NOVELTY-SATIATION dynamic—whether the model's drive to propose NEW ideas decays as it generates redundant ones, whether that decay is a decodable internal signal, and whether it CAUSES premature exploration collapse and failure. Prior exploration-in-LLMs work is behavioral (episode taxonomies) or locates static uncertainty representations; it never ties a satiating novelty signal to when the model stops generating diverse candidate strategies, nor causally reverses it. This differs from my prior overthinking proposals (which target stopping/verification/length under too-MUCH thinking) by targeting under-exploration—giving up idea-generation too soon—and its satiation mechanism.
Abstract: Humans keep exploring as long as new information feels novel, and satiate—stop seeking—once novelty fades. We ask whether reasoning language models exhibit an analog within a single chain of thought: as they generate candidate solution ideas, does an internal novelty drive decay with each redundant idea, causing them to stop proposing genuinely new approaches and commit prematurely to a familiar strategy? We call this novelty-satiation gating and hypothesize it is a distinct cause of reasoning failure: on problems whose first-considered strategy is wrong, a satiated model abandons idea-generation before reaching the approach that works. Across math (MATH500, AIME), science (GPQA), and open-ended exploration puzzles (a Little-Alchemy-2-style discovery task) on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we first segment traces into candidate-idea proposals, measure idea diversity over the trace, and show diversity decays and idea-generation halts earlier on failed than solved problems requiring strategy switches. We then test a mechanistic account: a linear probe on the residual stream at each idea boundary decodes a novelty/satiation signal that decays monotonically as similar ideas accumulate, is separable from a generic uncertainty or difficulty probe, and whose early decay predicts failure. We localize it, causally validate via activation patching (patch a high-novelty state into a satiated context and observe a fresh, distinct idea), and test a training-free 'novelty-refresh' steer that restores exploration when the signal collapses early. Our work reframes a class of reasoning failure as premature novelty satiation with a decodable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments: 1) Candidate-idea segmentation and diversity (behavioral): Segment CoT into candidate-idea proposals—spans where the model floats a distinct solution approach ('maybe try...', 'alternatively...', 'what if we use...')—via lexical cues plus an LLM-judge that clusters proposals into distinct strategy classes. Compute per-trace idea-diversity trajectory (number of NEW distinct strategies introduced per idea-boundary) and the idea-generation halt point (last boundary that introduces a novel strategy). Datasets: MATH500, AIME, GPQA, and a Little-Alchemy-2-style discovery puzzle (open-ended combination task where distinct 'ideas' = distinct combinations tried). Report diversity trajectories and halt points across models. 2) Satiation predicts failure (behavioral): Restrict to problems whose most-obvious first strategy is WRONG (identified by whether the model's first proposed strategy solves it; and by construction in templated 'strategy-switch-required' problems). Hypothesis: on these, failed traces satiate earlier (halt idea-generation sooner, lower late-trace diversity) than solved traces, whereas on first-strategy-correct problems satiation is harmless. Mixed-effects model of success on satiation timing controlling for problem identity/difficulty; compare against no-satiation and against the 'effort collapse' (total token) baseline to show satiation is distinct from just spending fewer tokens. 3) Novelty-satiation probing (Location): At each idea boundary, train a linear probe on the residual stream to decode a novelty signal—operationalized as whether the NEXT idea will be strategically novel vs redundant. Test whether the probe readout decays monotonically as redundant ideas accumulate within a trace (a satiation curve). Metrics: AUROC for next-idea-novelty, and slope of the satiation curve. Test separability from (a) a generic uncertainty/confidence probe and (b) a difficulty probe via principal angles and joint-model predictive gain; test whether early satiation-slope predicts final failure beyond uncertainty/difficulty. Layer sweep to localize (contrast with prior finding that uncertainty is early-layer). 4) Causal validation (Causal Intervention): Localize the novelty representation via activation patching; at a satiated idea boundary (probe below threshold), patch in a high-novelty state (from an early, non-satiated context) and test whether the model produces a genuinely NEW distinct strategy rather than repeating a familiar one. Controls: matched-random-direction patch (no effect), off-target accuracy preserved; report sign, dose-response, specificity. 5) Novelty-refresh steer (training-free intervention): Derive a novelty steering direction (difference-of-means between high- and low-novelty idea-boundary states). Online, when the probe detects early satiation on a still-unsolved problem, steer the novelty signal up to prompt a fresh, distinct approach. Evaluate on all datasets. Metrics: accuracy (especially on strategy-switch-required and first-strategy-wrong problems), idea-diversity recovery, added tokens, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy. Baselines: no intervention, self-consistency / higher-temperature resampling, prompting ('consider a completely different approach'), and the effort-forcing 'don't give up' nudge. Key claim: targeted novelty-refresh recovers accuracy on abandoned problems more token-efficiently than blunt resampling or effort forcing. 6) Failure/specificity analysis: verify the steer does not over-trigger on problems where the first strategy is correct (inducing wasteful exploration / overthinking) by gating on unsolved-state; measure accuracy/token cost on first-strategy-correct items. 7) Generalization: transfer probe and steer across datasets and model scales without retraining; test whether larger/RL-tuned models satiate later (a satiation analog of better exploration in stronger models).
Risk Factors and Limitations: Segmenting and clustering 'candidate ideas' into distinct strategies is noisy; we mitigate with lexical cues plus LLM-judge clustering and human spot-checks, anchoring the strongest claims on the discovery-puzzle and templated strategy-switch problems where distinct ideas are well-defined. Novelty satiation may be inseparable from a generic uncertainty or difficulty signal (a satiated model may simply be confident/stuck), which would weaken the distinct-mechanism claim; the separability analysis, monotonic within-trace satiation curve (a dynamical, not just magnitude, signature), and causal patching directly test this, and a null is an informative negative result. The phenomenon may only appear on problems requiring strategy switches; on first-strategy-correct problems early commitment is beneficial (this is the intended specificity, not a flaw). Steering could push activations off-distribution or induce wasteful exploration/overthinking on easy items; unsolved-state gating, matched-random-direction controls, and the specificity analysis quantify this trade-off. The novelty-refresh steer may not beat strong resampling baselines on accuracy alone, but the mechanistic reframing (a satiating novelty signal causing premature exploration collapse) is a standalone contribution. Reasoning-trace segmentation requires clear think/answer delimiters; LLM-judge clustering is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Effects may be model-family and scale specific.
